records.title: Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models
records.reason: Orca directly studies serving transformer-based generative models at scale. Its iteration-level scheduler and selective batching target autoregressive generation, and the full paper evaluates the system on GPT-3 and other large generative models; this is within LLM inference/serving scope.
records.body_check: Primary USENIX full text reviewed (OSDI 2022 PDF). Method: Orca schedules at iteration granularity and selectively batches requests so completed sequences do not force unnecessary work on other requests. Evaluation: Azure ND96asr A100 v4, 8 A100 40GB GPUs per VM and up to four VMs; GPT models include 13B and 175B, and the paper reports up to 36.9x higher throughput than FasterTransformer at the same latency. Limitations: results are tied to the evaluated hardware, models, workloads, and batch-size choices; the discussion says general scheduler/engine API design preserving abstraction is left for future work. The paper directly evaluates distributed generative-model serving.

records.title: Model Compression and Hardware Acceleration for Neural Networks: A Comprehensive Survey
records.reason: The full article copy shows a broad 2020 survey of general DNN compression and hardware acceleration, with the main categories compact models, tensor decomposition, quantization, and sparsification. It briefly mentions NAS for transformer architectures, but the surveyed methods and performance tables are not LLM/generative-transformer inference evaluations. The methods may transfer to LLM compression, yet direct coverage is not established; retain as borderline rather than accept or unrelated.
records.body_check: Reviewed the readable copy of the complete article (Proceedings of the IEEE, Vol. 108 No. 4, pp. 485–531; title, authors, DOI, pagination match the IEEE record). Method coverage: compact models, tensor decomposition, quantization, sparsification, and algorithm/hardware co-design; one NAS passage notes transformer architecture search. Evaluation: comparison tables cover general DNNs and accelerator performance, with examples dominated by CNNs/RNNs, image classification, speech, and edge deployment; no LLM or generative-serving evaluation was identified. Limitations: the authors caution that fair cross-paper comparison is difficult due to differing compression settings and hardware, and large-model compression/accuracy tradeoffs remain difficult. Source provenance note: article text was read through a public Scribd copy, not the IEEE-hosted copy; publisher DOI metadata was used to match article identity. Primary publisher full-text endpoint remained blocked by robot verification.

records.title: Speeding-up Convolutional Neural Networks Using Fine-tuned CP-Decomposition
records.reason: The primary abstract/full HTML studies CP-decomposition of convolution kernels to accelerate two vision CNNs, including AlexNet and a character-classification CNN. Its evaluations report CNN accuracy/speed trade-offs, not LLM inference, serving, or LLM-oriented compression; this is a clear scope mismatch.
records.body_check: Primary arXiv abstract and HTML text checked. The method decomposes a 4D convolution kernel into four smaller convolutional layers and fine-tunes the resulting CNN. The experiments use a character-classification CNN and AlexNet, reporting CPU speedup and classification-accuracy changes. The evaluated models and outcomes are vision/CNN-specific; no LLM inference or serving method is studied, so abstract-level exclusion is sufficient. Full text was not otherwise needed for this clear scope mismatch.
